name: Denmark
summary_text: Denmark is a historically progressive destination. It was the first European country to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration (2014), has banned conversion therapy (2023), offers nonbinary gender markers, and has comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering gender identity. There is no rollback movement, and Copenhagen ranks among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities. One documented weakness: the Danish Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that a trans woman who legally changed her gender but hasn't had surgery must serve in a men's prison and be strip-searched by male staff — finding this did not violate the European Convention on Human Rights. This is the same prison-placement issue documented in France, Germany, and the UK. The Danish Institute for Human Rights also flags that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time of reporting. Anti-trans discourse is intensifying (debate over lowering the LGR age limit; an opinion piece by a former equality minister presenting trans people as a threat to gender equality) but has not produced rollback legislation.

sources.title: Denmark's decade of self-ID cools debate on trans rights | Context by TRF
sources.claim_summary: Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Sept 2024): Denmark marks 10 years as the first European country with legal self-ID (2014); the debate has stayed cool - no criminal incidents recorded since the law passed, and even a contested prison-placement ruling failed to ignite a political storm. Denmark was also first to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989).

sources.title: Denmark | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): robust protections - marriage and adoption, SOGISC discrimination prohibited, self-determined legal gender markers, nonbinary 'X' passports, blood-donation rules based on practices not identity (July 2024), comprehensive LGBTIQ-inclusive sex education; 93% public support for same-sex relationships (Eurobarometer 2023).

sources.title: Transkønnet skal afsone på mandeafdeling, fastslår Højesteret - TV 2
sources.claim_summary: TV 2 (Sept 2024, in Danish): Denmark's Supreme Court ruled that a trans prisoner (legally changed gender in 2015, no surgery) must serve her sentence in a men's unit - the case passed without major political controversy.

sources.title: Discrimination and hatred | The Danish Institute for Human Rights
sources.claim_summary: Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT barometer page on discrimination and hatred - monitoring of discrimination and hate incidents against LGBT people in Denmark.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Denmark: anti-trans and anti-gender discourse intensified during the parliamentary debate on lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition (Christian sites accused trans groups of taking children 'hostage'); the UN Committee Against Torture flagged nonconsensual intersex surgeries; trans people and migrants reported being denied access to spaces and services.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Denmark: former equality minister Marie Bjerre published an opinion piece presenting trans and intersex people as a threat to gender equality (she was reassigned); in July a migrant trans woman was murdered in a Copenhagen hotel room; CAT concerns over intersex surgeries persist.

sources.title: Is Copenhagen Safe for LGBTQ+ Travel? 2026 Guide | Wandering With Pride
sources.claim_summary: WanderSafe LGBTQ+ travel safety page for Copenhagen (2026): safety confidence scores (LGBTQ+ 91, Trans 89 - 'Safe'); legal status summary (partnerships 1989, marriage 2012, self-declaration since 2014, conversion-therapy ban 2023); describes Copenhagen as compact, walkable and exceptionally safe.

sources.title: Denmark - F&M Global Barometers
sources.claim_summary: F&M Global Barometers country profile for Denmark: composite LGBT-rights perception scores including the Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

sources.title: Fernanda Milan, Guatemalan Transgender Woman, Granted Asylum In Denmark | HuffPost Voices
sources.claim_summary: HuffPost (Feb 2013): Fernanda Milan, a Guatemalan trans woman, became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark - she feared persecution for her trans activism in Guatemala (police attacks and threats); initially refused by the refugee appeals board, her case was reopened after LGBT Denmark provided documentation.
